content: 1. Indicators that support intersectoral coordination, such as those addressing gender equality, are essential for effective policy planning and monitoring. 2. The module facilitates the planning and monitoring of policies related to student selection, admission, enrollment, and teaching staff. 3. Module 3 focuses on education and training regulation and accreditation, supporting mechanisms to coordinate an intersectoral health workforce (HWF) agenda. 4. Indicators based on education regulations provide critical information on quality assurance and the requirements for education and training. 5. Accreditation mechanisms and their standards are crucial to ensure that national education plans for the health workforce align with the national health plan, ensuring that all health workers possess the skills needed to meet the population's needs. 6. An indicator on in-service training aims to align health sector training with broader educational policies and programs, including technical and vocational education and training, within a lifelong learning framework. 7. These indicators enhance the quality and relevance of HWF education and training and identify areas for intervention in the regulation or management of education and training. 8. Module 4 addresses education financing, aiming to support an effective financing architecture that strengthens intersectoral collaboration between health and education sectors and promotes investment in lifelong learning systems. 9. Data from this module can support retention policies, advance understanding of targeted investments for equitable access to education and lifelong learning opportunities, and identify adequate budgetary resources for transformative education, skills development, and job creation. 10. Module 5 measures entries to and exits from the health labor market, differentiating between domestic efforts and reliance on foreign health workers, while monitoring voluntary and involuntary exits. 11. Information on the balance of the health labor market is gathered by tracking vacancies and unemployment, with disaggregation at subnational levels where possible. 12. Understanding the magnitude and drivers of workforce flows provides a foundation for effective recruitment and retention policies. 13. Module 6 addresses employment characteristics and working conditions, facilitating the implementation and review of causal and descriptive labor market analyses. 14. The distribution of health workers by working time and labor market characteristics is essential for understanding HWF dynamics and builds upon initiatives like International Labor Standards on working time and work-life balance. 15. Indicators on working conditions contribute to progress toward achieving decent work for all, as promoted by Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6. 16. Module 7 maps expenditures on the health workforce and remuneration in the health sector, including earnings in the private sector where relevant. 17. Data on these indicators contribute to decent work (SDG 6) and gender equality (SDG 5), involving collaboration with ministries of finance, labor, and education, as well as private sector representatives. 18. Module 8 focuses on skill mix composition for models of care, emphasizing the availability of skilled health workers in various settings to achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC). 19. Indicators in this module analyze the structure of the workforce by sector and occupational group, providing insights into how labor supply matches healthcare needs and population composition. 20. Aligning skill mix to case mix is critical for improving and integrating patient-centered care by doctors, nurses, and allied professionals, with a focus on primary care services. 21. Module 9 includes governance and health workforce policy indicators, assessing whether a country can coordinate an intersectoral HWF agenda and has a central HWF unit. 22. Indicators on health workforce policies evaluate whether a country has processes to plan for the health workforce, aligns education plans with the national health plan, and has institutional models to assess healthcare staffing needs. 23. This module demonstrates whether a country effectively uses and applies information collected under other module indicators. 24. Module 10 defines indicators on the status of human resources for health information systems (HRHIS), data management, and their alignment with international reporting requirements for tracking the health workforce. 25. Indicators assess whether the national HRHIS can track outputs from education and training institutions, labor market entrants, active workforce stock, labor market exits, and geocoded health facility locations. 26. The implementation of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is a country-led activity, leveraging national systems and existing mechanisms to coordinate data collection for evaluating the health workforce. 27. WHO has developed tools, including a handbook, implementation guide, and web platform, to assist countries in implementing the NHWA. 28. WHO regional offices provide direct support for NHWA implementation and respond to country-specific queries. 29. NHWA indicators include both numeric and capability metrics, offering information on regulation and mechanisms related to the health workforce. 30. Annual monitoring of NHWA indicators is expected, with reporting covering a one-year period. 31. Measurements may be cross-sectional, cumulative, or based on flows of individuals from a cohort, with careful consideration of denominators for inflow and outflow indicators. 32. Disaggregation of indicators is necessary, with factors defined to harmonize data collection. Progressive implementation allows for monitoring and reporting of more complex disaggregation levels over time. 33. Subnational disaggregation is recommended based on administrative units, such as states, regions, or districts, without overlaps. 34. Financial indicators should use national currency for local reporting and standardized US dollars for international reporting, with mid-year conversion rates applied for annual sums. 35. Population estimates for density indicators should use standard international estimates, such as those from the United Nations Population Division, for global comparisons. 36. Indicators for NHWA are defined by health workforce occupations, following the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08). 37. Countries are encouraged to register detailed information at the ISCO-08 unit level to improve HWF statistics. 38. While NHWA primarily focuses on health workers, countries are encouraged to track data on social workers employed in health facilities for a comprehensive overview of health-related activities. 39. Member States are encouraged to report data even if national definitions deviate from NHWA standards, with deviations clearly documented.
